title: I finally don’t care about them
author: BSwayzeYo
selftext: Hey y’all. I don’t know if you’ve noticed yet, but they (the haters), really don’t matter much anymore. Their numbers are shrinking, they are having to scream louder and louder, the content creators can’t avoid including games made with ai without risking their livelihoods, and it sure seems to me like at least 50% of today’s hate comments are just fake news from bot farms trying to drive engagement. It’s almost over. They’re almost done. Plough on my friends. 🏌️🎣😎🎉

replies.author: Aromatic-Low-4578

People want to be able to build game and have them judged on merit, simple as that.

replies.author: OkVariety8064
replies.body:
> People want to be able to build game and have them judged on merit, simple as that.

If anyone can build their game with just a few prompts, why would anyone want your game specifically? And even if they do, their very own improved version is just a few prompts away.

> People want to be respected for their output, not hated on for their choice of tool.

If it stops being your output to the degree it is trivially easy for anyone to make something similar, why would anyone respect your for that?

> We all know a wave of slop is coming, no defending that but there has always been slop in gaming, it just went from asset flips to low quality slapped together AI games.

You hope for AI development to get to the point where literally anyone can build a game. Currently, the cost of tools (engines and so on) is pretty much zero, but there is still the limiting factor of skill. Once that is gone, what will be left?

Seriously, what will be left? Prompting isn't exactly a complex skill and AI can help with that too. If the cost (tools, skills and opportunity) gets lowered to the point where *literally anyone* can get the AI to build a game, what is left? Anything interesting will be cloned within hours. Games will be the equal of memes, something thrown together in a few hours and endlessly varied and copied.

No on will respect you, just like no one respects the original author of a meme. They will only care about posting their take on it.

Or are you perhaps hoping that AI will advance to a level *just complicated enough* for you but not everyone else to use it, and then you will find fame and fortune as the bestest AI prompter there is? Good luck with that.

replies.author: johnesco
replies.body:
Yes AI is a different tool because of what it can generate, but it generates base on what it's been trained on. Coming up with new ideas, for now, is still a very human thing and many people just trying to copy will eventually hit copyright issues.

Think about how as computer prices dropped and even stand alone word processors like the Smith Corona came to market, now everyone can write a book right? Do they? Or do they write resumes, recipes, little things meant only for them. Being able to type your own things didn't replace books. Being able to prompt out a book will also not replace books. A book is still the taste and organization of the writer. 

Anyone being "able" to is still not the same as everyone have to time, ideas and follow through to do it.

I'm not saying it's easy for devs, but it's going to get MUCH more difficult getting noticed. I love these tools and everybody should have an opportunity to create, but the rat race is going to get bigger.

replies.author: Bruoche
replies.body:
I think there's nuance to be had between expecting creators to design their games and creator manufacturing their games. 

If you're doing the design in great detail and AI just translate your specs into code without any interpretation it's one thing, using AI to one shot prompt a vague game concept is very different then just using a factory to industrialise the distribution of your game. 

Factories are made to make sure things are made faster, but also more reliably. They allow making sure every board game sold would hopefully have the same quality in line with the designer's intent.

AI on the other hand doesn't make sure to manufacture intent, it produces likely satisfactory results based on a prompt. On it's face that's similar but if you're not being very specific most of the game made will just be AI's 'best guess'

replies.author: bubuplush
replies.body:
I'm not even heavily against AI (except when they just wrote a prompt or 'stole' insanely good art and 'slop' it into something ugly only to sell it) but it feels ridiculous at this point. Yesterday I wrote 3 sentences into Claude, told it to make a pixel art side scroller where you play a mage with 4 spells. "give it cool fancy pixel explosion effects" lmao. It pumped out an insanely good game with music, good basic UI design and nice-looking character sprites.

Idk I know that it'll be a normal thing in the future, but I felt a bit.. dirty and cheap doing this? Like there was pretty much no creative process involved. I feel like a kid that taps the paper with a pencil and a Mona Lisa appears within the blink of an eye. Maybe the Mona Lisa has a weird-looking eye, but almost no one would notice. ... Yay..? Like right now I can just type the most basic prompts ever, or even ask an AI to come up with unique ideas, and flood the market with 20 simple, yet visually bombastic (for average users) phone games.

comments.author: CandidateDue2480
comments.body:
You do your thang, everyone should try to make greatness out of every tool that comes into existence. 

I'm a game dev with 10+ years and many shipped games, I'm using AI for many things that replace how I used to work. I'll tell you that on the other side of having the skills to build its quite depressing as a workflow. I can see how exciting it is to open doors for people who didn't have the skills - moreso than any of the last generations of tool developments.

But I will be curious how people feel after their initial excitement at being able to make a thing fades, and they put in the many hard years of iteration required to make a game that is both critically well-received, and sells well. So far AI isn't finishing games to the level of hitting good, shippable, widely adopted status. Because the last 20% of finishing a game is harder than the first 80% combined, and it's not even close.

There's certainly AI adoption in parts of core games development, and that will grow on the art side over time. The tech side is rife with it.

As it stands, that no AI game has come to market that is a critical success. I'm sure there's some commercial success by now, but nothing newsworthy as we'd see it everywhere from huge AI proponents.

Ultimately making a great game is still as hard as its ever been. I hope people enjoy doing what they're doing, and we'll see what happens as people start hitting the harder parts of production.

  
Good luck!
